lessons.title: A five-step audit of your organisation's AI systems
lessons.subtitle: From existing records to a prioritised gap list

sections.title: Five steps for a defensible initial inventory
sections.content:
Nobody can tell you how long your AI inventory will take. It depends on the organisation, the number of systems, shadow IT, supplier records, and the risk profile. The five steps below are a working method, not a promise that one week or a fixed number of hours will be enough.

**1. Build the inventory.** The record of processing activities under Article 30 GDPR is one source for AI-supported processing of personal data. One. Add IT asset and SaaS registers, procurement records, supplier contracts, billing records, browser or SSO approvals, and structured interviews, because only those turn up systems without personal data and shadow AI.

**2. Establish the purpose and system boundary.** Write down which function is actually running. A product name says neither whether a function uses AI nor what its intended purpose is.

**3. Determine the role and possible risk class.** Per system: prohibited practice under Article 5, high-risk under Article 6 with Annex I or III, transparency case under Article 50, or none of those specific categories. Applicable exceptions and application dates belong on the same sheet.

**4. Collect evidence and assess gaps.** Provider information, contracts, instructions for use, data flows, oversight, logs, security, and the duties that apply to the particular use case. Article 26 reaches only deployers of high-risk systems, Article 50 only its own specific conditions.

**5. Prioritise measures.** Every evidenced gap gets a responsible person, a deadline, a dependency, and a verification criterion. The review cadence follows risk, change, and legal developments, not a generic quarterly rule.
sections.keyTakeaway: A GDPR record of processing activities is a way in, not an AI inventory. Technical, contractual, and organisational sources come on top, and what gets classified is the actual use case.

sections.title: An inventory with traceable fields
sections.content:
The AI Act prescribes no spreadsheet format for deployers and no list of 14 mandatory columns. Take the tool that keeps responsibilities, access rights, and changes manageable.

**Useful fields:** system ID, name, version, provider, function actually used, intended and internal purpose, user groups, affected persons, data categories, integrations, your role, possible risk category with a rationale, relevant duties, approval status, responsible person, contractual and provider evidence, human oversight, logging, security controls, DPIA or FRIA status where applicable, incidents, last review, and next trigger.

Reconcile the inventory with records of processing activities and DPIAs, with IT asset and SaaS management, procurement, supplier contracts, SSO and browser approvals, the business units, and the reporting routes for shadow AI.

Versioning and change history are good governance controls. Whether the law requires them, and in what form, follows from the role and the duty. A spreadsheet alone is not evidence of compliance.
sections.keyTakeaway: There is no prescribed 14-column template. The inventory has to make the real system purpose, role, classification, evidence, responsibilities, and changes traceable.

sections.title: Review questions that produce useful evidence
sections.content:
Typical risks are review questions, not findings about your own organisation.

- **Which generative services are actually running?** Article 4 requires context-appropriate measures to support AI literacy. Article 50 bites only where its specific transparency condition is met.
- **Which HR function is active?** An AI system that reviews, filters, or evaluates job applications may fall within Annex III, point 4(a). A brand name and an AI claim are not enough for the classification.
- **Is there use outside approved accounts?** Check that with lawful, proportionate sources and a secure reporting route.
- **Does a high-risk system generate logs, and does the deployer control them?** Article 26(6) governs retention of the automatically generated logs under the deployer's control.
- **Are current provider information and the instructions for use available?** Do not claim that a provider delivers within days. Request, review, and version what is actually supplied.

The prioritised gap list follows from evidenced answers and the correct classification. From nothing else.
sections.keyTakeaway: Verify instead of assuming. Active function, intended purpose, approved use, applicable duties, logs, and current provider records.

quiz.questionText: An organisation uses an AI system whose intended purpose is to review and filter job applications for recruitment. Which classification must it assess?

answerOptions.text: Minimal risk, with no obligations
Limited risk, with only a transparency duty under Article 50
High-risk under Annex III, point 4(a)
Prohibited under Article 5

quiz.explanation: Annex III, point 4(a), names AI systems intended for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to analyse and filter job applications. The final classification needs the specific intended purpose and an assessment under Article 6, including any possible exception under Article 6(3).

quiz.questionText: For how long must a deployer retain automatically generated logs of a high-risk AI system?

answerOptions.text: At least 30 days
At least three months
At least six months
Indefinitely, for as long as the system operates

quiz.explanation: Article 26(6) requires automatically generated logs to be kept for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, and at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about a record of processing activities under Article 30 GDPR as a source for an AI inventory is correct?

answerOptions.text: It automatically contains every AI system, including systems that do not process personal data
It is a useful starting point for AI-supported processing of personal data, but must be supplemented with technical, contractual, and organisational sources
It removes the need to review IT assets, procurement, suppliers, and business units
It already proves the correct AI Act risk class

quiz.explanation: A record of processing activities makes processing of personal data visible. That is all. It captures neither every AI system nor every active function or shadow AI, and it does not replace an inventory of systems, procurement, and business-unit use.

lessons.title: Connecting the GDPR, ISO 42001, and ISO 23894
lessons.subtitle: What you already have, and what is genuinely new

sections.title: Using a DPIA as a starting point
sections.content:
A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) under Article 35 GDPR replaces no duty under the AI Act. It makes information reusable, and that is all. Article 26(9) requires deployers of high-risk systems to use the information supplied by the provider under Article 13 when carrying out a DPIA where one is required. How large the overlap is depends on the system, the data, and the available documentation. Fixed coverage percentages are not reliable.

**Assess separately:**
- **GDPR:** legal basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, data-subject rights, processing on behalf of a controller, transfers, security, and Article 35.
- **Deployer obligations under Article 26:** instructions for use, human oversight, input data where controlled by the deployer, monitoring and response, logs where controlled by the deployer, information for employees, and further duties depending on the use case.
- **Provider obligations:** among them the conformity assessment and the EU declaration of conformity. A deployer does not issue that declaration merely because it uses the system.
- **Article 4:** context-appropriate measures to support AI literacy. The provision prescribes neither a particular training plan nor a certificate. Internal records make implementation traceable.

Article 27(4) permits the entities within its scope to conduct a FRIA together with a DPIA. The distinct subject matter of each assessment must still be covered.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 26(9) links provider information to a DPIA where one is required. It creates no fixed coverage ratio, and it replaces neither AI Act nor GDPR analysis.

sections.title: ISO 42001 and ISO 23894 as structural aids
sections.content:
**ISO/IEC 42001:2023** can structure a management system for roles, objectives, risks, controls, monitoring, and improvement. **ISO/IEC 23894:2023** supplies guidance for AI risk management. Whether individual provisions fit your role and your system has to be assessed on the merits.

Certification to ISO/IEC 42001 creates no presumption of conformity under the AI Act. The presumption under Article 40 attaches to relevant harmonised standards, or parts of them, whose references are published in the Official Journal of the European Union. Draft designations and procedural status change; check the current Official Journal and the official standardisation information.

Use management standards as a frame. Map every control to the specific legal role and duty, and claim no presumption of conformity without the official reference.
sections.keyTakeaway: ISO 42001 and ISO 23894 can structure governance and risk management. Certification and an AI Act presumption of conformity are separate questions.

sections.title: The crosswalk: identifying additional work
sections.content:
A crosswalk saves duplicate work when it puts common ground and differences side by side.

- A record of processing activities feeds personal-data AI processing in; an AI inventory needs further sources.
- A DPIA can be prepared together with a FRIA where a FRIA is required. It replaces neither the FRIA nor deployer obligations.
- A data-processing agreement under Article 28 GDPR applies only to processing on behalf of a controller. Procurement assurances and AI Act assurances are assessed separately by role and system.
- Documentation of technical and organisational measures can reuse security controls. Article 15 addresses providers of high-risk systems; deployers have their own Article 26 and data-protection duties.
- Information under Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and under Article 26(11) of the AI Act has different conditions and different content.
- The data protection officer may be involved. The AI Act does not require an “AI officer”; responsibility, independence, and conflicts of interest are settled deliberately.

**Review fields that may come on top:** deployer logs under Article 26(6), employee information under paragraph 7, EU database duties according to role, context-appropriate Article 4 measures, and response to risks and incidents under Article 26(5). The reporting duty and periods in Article 73 address providers; deployers settle their own information and escalation path.

For Article 22 GDPR, check precisely whether a solely automated decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects a person, whether an exception applies, and which safeguards are required.
sections.keyTakeaway: A crosswalk shows reuse and gaps without mixing roles. Data protection officer and AI responsibility, provider and deployer duties, GDPR and AI Act analysis stay separate.

quiz.questionText: Which standard is being prepared as a harmonised European standard for the quality-management system under Article 17 of the EU AI Act?

answerOptions.text: prEN 18286

quiz.explanation: prEN 18286 is the coming harmonised European standard for the quality-management system under Article 17. ISO 42001 is an international standard without an Annex ZA, and therefore without a presumption of conformity under the AI Act.

quiz.questionText: You already have a DPIA under Article 35 GDPR for a CV-screening system. Does it replace the obligations under Article 26 of the EU AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Yes. The DPIA covers every AI Act obligation.

No. The DPIA may support the analysis but does not replace AI Act duties. Logging and human-oversight duties may apply to the deployer, while data and conformity-assessment duties must be assigned according to the provider and deployer roles.
No. A DPIA is entirely unrelated to the AI Act.
Only a DPIA more than 24 months old must be supplemented.

quiz.explanation: A DPIA can make information reusable, but it has no fixed coverage ratio. Article 26(9) requires provider information to be used for a DPIA where one is required. Deployer duties and provider duties, such as the conformity assessment, are allocated separately.

quiz.questionText: Which article of the EU AI Act expressly refers to a DPIA under Article 35 GDPR?

answerOptions.text: Article 13(3)
Article 26(9)
Article 27(1)
Article 35(2)

quiz.explanation: Article 26(9) of the EU AI Act has deployers use the information from Article 13 in order to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 GDPR where one is required. No automatic DPIA duty for every AI use follows from that, and no replacement of the AI Act duties.

lessons.title: Templates and checklists
lessons.subtitle: How to classify and maintain working templates

sections.title: A governance package ordered by priority
sections.content:
Build the governance package in this order. The AI acceptable-use policy first, then risk classification, the Article 4 training framework, the DPIA worksheet, provider due diligence, the AI inventory, the pilot charter, and last the use-case assessment matrix.

These documents are implementation tools, not statutory forms, and none of them proves compliance. Article 4 requires context-appropriate measures to support AI literacy, but neither a particular training plan nor a certificate. A DPIA is mandatory only where the conditions in Article 35 GDPR are met. Risk classification and deployer duties follow from the specific system and role, not from filling in a file.

Build every document as a working structure: bring in the responsible subject-matter roles, substantiate claims, record the reasons for decisions, check the current law, adapt it to the use case. How much work and coordination that costs cannot be pinned to a single weekend.
sections.keyTakeaway: The eight documents are working structures you build yourself, not prescribed legal forms, and they prove no compliance. Duties and evidence follow from the system, the role, and the context.

sections.title: What working templates may contain
sections.content:
**AI acceptable-use policy.** Scope, permitted and excluded use cases, data classes, approval routes, human review, rights, incidents, contacts, change process. A file of that name is not something the AI Act requires.

**Article 4 working framework.** Record role, prior knowledge, context of use, affected persons, and risks, and derive the learning, instruction, and control measures from that. The Commission is clear: no single mandatory format, no prescribed minimum number of hours, no mandatory certificate. Internal records make implementation traceable.

**Procurement and contract checklist.** Review fields are provider information under Article 13, intended purpose, system version, performance limits, updates, logs, security, support, incidents, data processing, exit arrangements, and the necessary evidence. Audit rights, contractual penalties, reporting cycles, or a German-language requirement are negotiation points, not clauses prescribed universally by law.

**Incident-response worksheet.** Separate deployer duties from provider duties. Where a deployer identifies a risk or a serious incident, Article 26(5) governs notification and suspension of use. The reporting duty and the periods for providers of high-risk systems sit in Article 73. The competent authority and the reporting route depend on the current national implementation and on the sector.
sections.keyTakeaway: Templates contain context-dependent review fields. Article 4 knows neither mandatory hours nor a mandatory certificate, and contract clauses and incident roles are not prescribed uniformly.

sections.title: Storage and maintenance responsibilities
sections.content:
**Storage.** Take a controlled system with clear owners, appropriate access rights, versioning, retention, and recovery. Git or SharePoint can be that; the AI Act prescribes neither.

**Maintenance.** Name a responsible function. An “AI officer” is not something the AI Act requires. Review on changes to the system, purpose, provider, model, data, an incident, or the law, plus a risk-appropriate interval. A generic quarterly cadence is not an authority-mandated rule.

**Sources.**
- EUR-Lex and the European Commission for the text of the Regulation, its timeline, guidance, and AI-literacy questions and answers.
- Data-protection supervisory authorities for GDPR guidance.
- The competent national and sectoral authorities for current enforcement and reporting information.

Substantiate decisions about real systems. Length, file format, or version history alone prove nothing.
sections.keyTakeaway: Controlled storage, clear responsibility, and event- and risk-based maintenance. Check the current law against primary sources.

quiz.questionText: What is the legal status of internally created working templates for governance records?

answerOptions.text: They are adaptable working tools. The AI Act does not prescribe particular filenames or formats, and the applicable duties must be assessed for each system and role.
Four documents are always mandatory and four are always voluntary.
All eight documents are prescribed EU forms.
Completing all eight documents automatically proves compliance.

quiz.explanation: The templates help with inventory work, classification, AI-literacy measures, data protection, and procurement. Nobody prescribes their filename or their format. Whether a specific duty such as a DPIA bites depends on its own statutory conditions.

quiz.questionText: How often should governance records be reviewed according to this lesson?

answerOptions.text: After changes to the system, purpose, provider, model, data, incidents, or law, and additionally at a risk-appropriate interval; a fixed quarterly cadence is not prescribed by an authority.
Exactly once per quarter, as required by law.
Only during an authority inspection.
Never, once the records have been created.

quiz.explanation: The AI Act prescribes no fixed review frequency. Triggers are changes to the system, purpose, provider, model, or data, an incident, or a legal change, supplemented by a risk-appropriate interval.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about Article 73 is correct for a serious incident resulting in death?

answerOptions.text: Two days
The provider of a high-risk system must report immediately after establishing the causal link, and no later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident; deployers also follow Article 26(5).
15 days
72 hours

quiz.explanation: Article 73 addresses the report to providers of high-risk systems. Where a person dies, the report is due immediately after the causal link or its reasonable likelihood is established, and no later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident. Deployers have their own notification and suspension duties under Article 26(5).

lessons.title: Case study: an SME introduces a CV-screening tool
lessons.subtitle: A decision path through the Regulation
keyConcepts: section 87 of the German Works Constitution Act
three separate issues under the German General Equal Treatment Act

sections.title: Classification and duties under Article 26
sections.content:
**Fictional facts:** XY GmbH, a machinery manufacturer in Bavaria with 200 employees. The managing director buys a CV-screening system whose intended purpose is to rank CVs by a match score and prepare a shortlist. No real product, no real function.

**Step 1, assessment against Article 5.** The described purpose is none of the practices listed there. The specific implementation still has to be assessed.

**Step 2, high-risk assessment under Article 6 and Annex III.** Point 4(a) covers AI for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to analyse and filter job applications. That is exactly the use case. Any exception under Article 6(3) and its conditions is assessed separately.

**Roles and timeline.** XY GmbH uses the system and is therefore the deployer. The supplier stays the provider as long as no change of role under Article 25 occurs. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, sets **2 December 2027** as the application date for the high-risk rules governing standalone Annex III systems.

**Deployer obligations once the system is deployed as high-risk and the rules apply:**
- Paragraph 1: appropriate technical and organisational measures for use in accordance with the instructions.
- Paragraphs 2 and 3: human oversight by competent, properly qualified and trained persons with the necessary authority and support; watch automation bias.
- Paragraph 4: input data the deployer controls must be relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose.
- Paragraph 5: monitor operation; where there is reason to consider that use may result in a risk, or where a serious incident is identified, inform the provider or distributor and the competent market-surveillance authority and suspend use.
- Paragraph 6: retain automatically generated logs under the deployer's control for at least six months, unless applicable law provides otherwise.
- Paragraph 7: before workplace use, inform workers' representatives and the affected workers.
- Paragraph 9: use provider information for a DPIA where one is required under Article 35 GDPR. Article 26(9) does not turn that into a DPIA duty for every HR system.
- Paragraph 11: inform affected persons when the high-risk system makes or assists in making decisions concerning them.
sections.keyTakeaway: From the binding application date of 2 December 2027, Annex III, point 4(a), can trigger the Article 26 catalogue for this use case.

sections.title: What XY GmbH does not have to do solely because of this use: Article 27 FRIA
sections.content:
**FRIA:** Article 27(1) covers deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of specified systems under Annex III, point 5(b) and (c). A private machinery manufacturer using the described HR case only for its own recruitment does not fall under Article 27 for that reason alone. Employment AI under Annex III, point 4, is not listed there as a separate private-sector FRIA category.

The DPIA is a different question. Article 35 GDPR requires one where the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Article 26(9) builds a bridge to the provider information, not an automatic DPIA duty.

**Keep provider and deployer apart.**
- The conformity assessment under Article 43 and the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 sit with the provider, as long as no change of role under Article 25 shifts duties. The deployer checks documentation, marking, and the instructions for use.
- Providers of Annex III high-risk systems have registration tasks under Article 49. Article 26(8) additionally requires deployers that are Union authorities, institutions, or bodies to register. A private deployer is not subject to registration merely because it uses the system.

**Parallel law in the fictional case.**
- **Section 87(1), point 6, of the German Works Constitution Act (BetrVG):** co-determination can apply where the statutory conditions are met and a works council exists. Procedure and legal consequence belong in an employment-law assessment.
- **German General Equal Treatment Act (AGG):** discrimination can trigger claims under section 15 and the evidential rule in section 22. Amount and limits depend on the claim and the facts; “uncapped” is not a reliable blanket statement.
- **Article 22 GDPR:** assess whether a decision is based solely on automated processing and produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects a person, whether an exception applies, and which safeguards are required. A merely formal human step does not reliably remove the solely automated character.

The AI Act, the GDPR, the AGG, and co-determination law can apply side by side, each with its own conditions.
sections.keyTakeaway: For the private HR use described, no FRIA follows from Article 27 alone. The DPIA, co-determination, the AGG, and Article 22 GDPR each remain to be assessed against their own conditions.

sections.title: Procurement review fields for the fictional system
sections.keyTakeaway: No blanket eight-clause catalogue. Procurement has to secure provider records and the update, logging, security, incident, and exit support the specific deployment needs.

quiz.questionText: A machinery manufacturer with 200 employees introduces Personio with AI-based applicant ranking. Must it conduct a fundamental-rights impact assessment (FRIA) under Article 27 of the EU AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Yes. Every deployment of high-risk AI triggers a FRIA.
No. Article 27(1) applies to public authorities, private entities providing public services, and deployers of systems under Annex III, point 5(b) or (c). Point 4 is not included.
Yes, because HR AI affects fundamental rights.
No, because a DPIA under Article 35 GDPR replaces the FRIA completely.

quiz.explanation: Article 27(1) does not cover the private employer described here merely because of HR AI under Annex III, point 4. A DPIA is assessed separately under Article 35 GDPR; Article 26(9) does not make it automatic.

quiz.questionText: Which Article 26 duty applies specifically to an employer before a high-risk AI system is put into service at work?

answerOptions.text: Article 26(2): human oversight
Article 26(6): keeping logs for six months
Article 26(7): informing workers' representatives and affected workers
Article 26(11): informing applicants

quiz.explanation: Article 26(7) requires an employer, before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at work, to inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the system. That is independent of co-determination under the Works Constitution Act.

quiz.questionText: Which areas of law require separate assessment for the fictional AI applicant-screening use case?

answerOptions.text: Only the EU AI Act; it displaces all other law.
The EU AI Act, the GDPR including Articles 22 and 35 where their conditions are met, the AGG, and co-determination under the Works Constitution Act where applicable.
The EU AI Act and GDPR; the AGG does not apply to AI.
Only the GDPR and Works Constitution Act; the AI Act does not apply until 2027.

quiz.explanation: The AI Act, the GDPR, the AGG, and the Works Constitution Act can apply side by side. Articles 22 and 35 GDPR, co-determination rights, and claims under the AGG each have their own conditions and consequences; none of them follows from the label “AI” alone.
